#3324. 8 Sci-Fi Miniseries That Are Bangers From Start to Finish

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Sci-fi shows have a habit of getting carried away with their own ideas. Give a series time travel, alien civilizations, or a machine that can predict the future, and suddenly every conversation becomes an excuse to explain how the technology works. The characters get buried under complicated theories, and by the time the story becomes interesting, it’s hard to care who survives. That’s a shame, because the best science fiction has always been about people, not the impossible things happening around them.

Fortunately, some miniseries understand that distinction better than others. They use their wildest concepts to tell surprisingly personal stories about grief, love, family, and the choices people make when their world stops making sense. And because these stories have a beginning and an actual ending, every episode has a reason to exist. Here are 8 sci-fi miniseries that are bangers from start to finish.

Childhood’s End opens with ships appearing above the world’s major cities. Karellen (Charles Dance) promises an end to war through Ricky Stormgren (Mike Vogel), the farmer chosen to meet him. He keeps his face hidden, so Ricky’s private conversations with the Overlord leave him with questions humanity cannot put directly to its new ruler.

Then the story jumps forward. Jake (Ashley Zukerman) and Amy Morrel (Hayley Magnus) watch their children develop abilities they cannot explain. Their world has peace and abundance, but they cannot raise their children into adulthood or share what the children are becoming. That shift, from a farmer asking one alien for answers to parents who have no one to ask, is why this show hurts. And that ending? Man, it really knows how to make a perfect world feel like the worst possible nightmare.

A key opens any door into the same motel room. A comb can stop time, and a bus ticket sends its holder elsewhere. That's the kind of bizarre mystery The Lost Room throws you into, and somehow, it only gets stranger. Detective Joe Miller (Peter Krause) finds these objects after a murder investigation leads him to Room 10 at the abandoned Sunshine Motel. Then his daughter Anna (Elle Fanning) disappears inside the room.

Other people want the key because it gives them control over every door. But, Joe wants it because Anna is gone. His search takes him through the private rules and rival groups that have formed around the objects, but the strange powers never matter as much as a father checking another empty room. And that's what makes this whole thing so gripping. Joe has no time to fall apart while he tries the next key, the next clue, the next door. For all its mysteries, the series comes down to one painfully simple thing. A father just wants his daughter back.

Cyberpunk: Edgerunners follows Gloria (Gloria Garayua), who takes extra emergency shifts to keep David (Zach Aguilar) at Arasaka Academy. After an ambulance crash kills her, he finds the military Sandevistan among the cyberware she stole from bodies at work. He installs it in his spine and uses it against the classmates who torment him.

Lucy (Emi Lo) shows him a braindance of the moon. She wants to go there for real, and David makes getting her there his goal. Maine (William C. Stephens) loses control, David adds more implants, and Lucy begs him to stop. Each dose of immunosuppressants helps him keep using the Sandevistan, but it cannot protect him forever. And here's what makes Cyberpunk: Edgerunners so damn heartbreaking. Lucy actually makes it to the moon, just like she always wanted. But David isn't there, and suddenly, getting everything she dreamed of doesn't feel like much of a victory.

Can a three-day pill trial help with heartbreak? Maniac takes that ridiculous question surprisingly seriously, which is pretty impressive for a show where two strangers keep waking up in increasingly bizarre versions of reality. Annie (Emma Stone) joins hoping to revisit the last car ride with her sister Ellie (Julia Garner), while Owen (Jonah Hill), recently fired, is pressured by his family to deny his schizophrenia diagnosis. At Neberdine, the pills send them into staged roles as thieves, spies, and strangers who keep meeting.

Their waking selves barely speak, while the drug scenarios repeatedly place them together. Annie relives her argument with Ellie before the crash, while Owen tries to work out whether his brother’s legal trouble is real or part of his illness. Annie and Owen make each fantasy funny enough to enjoy, then seem visibly drained when the pills wear off. When Annie decides Owen should not be left alone, it feels earned because she knows what it is to be dismissed while trying to explain that she is in pain.

Russell Keys (Steve Burton) returns from a World War II mission with missing time and nightmares nobody believes. Meanwhile, Owen Crawford (Joel Gretsch) sees the Roswell crash as a career opportunity and helps bury what happened. Sally Clarke (Catherine Dent) meets an alien while trapped in an unhappy marriage, then raises a daughter whose origins she cannot explain.

Back home, Russell’s wife and son live with his fear, while Owen’s choices cost him his family’s trust. Sally protects Allie (Dakota Fanning) from adults who see her as evidence. Taken follows their families for five decades, with children and grandchildren growing up around secrets their parents will not explain. And that's the crazy thing about this show. You've got aliens, government cover-ups, and decades of mystery, yet the people doing the most damage to these families are often the ones sitting right across the dinner table.

In 11.22.63 a diner’s back room gives Jake Epping (James Franco) one rule. Walk through the door and arrive in 1960, then return to the present and the past resets. He is there to stop Kennedy’s assassination. In Jodie, Texas, he meets Sadie (Sarah Gadon), a school librarian who notices how often his phrases sound wrong for the year.

While Jake is tracking Oswald (Daniel Webber), he and Sadie have built a life together. He keeps November 22 in mind and withholds what he is risking, and every decision protects the mission at her expense. After the timeline resets, Jake finds the elderly Sadie at a dance. She does not recognize him. He asks for one dance without telling her that he was the man she loved.

Station Eleven opens with Arthur Leander (Gael García Bernal) collapsing onstage while playing King Lear. In the audience, Jeevan (Himesh Patel) tries to help. Kirsten (Matilda Lawler), an eight-year-old actor, watches. Later that night she asks Jeevan to take her home. Then the flu spreads, and the two are stuck trying to make a safe life in an apartment with Jeevan’s brother Frank (Nabhaan Rizwan).

Twenty years later, Kirsten (Mackenzie Davis) is with the Traveling Symphony, performing Shakespeare for communities that have survived. She still carries the Station Eleven comic Arthur gave her, with drawings and lines she knows by heart. The airport story gives Clark (David Wilmot) a different emergency of keeping strangers fed, calm, and willing to live together. The series shifts focus among survivors’ losses. When Kirsten and Jeevan find each other again, the relief hits before either of them speaks.

In Devs, Sergei (Karl Glusman) gets one day inside a secretive development division. Lily (Sonoya Mizuno) knows he wouldn’t simply leave, but Forest (Nick Offerman) and security chief Kenton (Zach Grenier) have already settled on the explanation she is supposed to accept. She looks for answers inside Amaya’s sealed development building, where a quantum computer reconstructs events in unnerving detail.

Forest lost his daughter Amaya and built a system that lets him watch versions of her again. He insists the universe has only one possible course, but Lily refuses his account of Sergei’s death. One man wants proof that the daughter he lost still exists somewhere, while one woman wants the truth about the person she loved. And the really unsettling part is that Forest has a machine capable of looking into the past, yet Lily still has to fight just to get a straight answer about what happened to Sergei.

#3322. Star Trek 60th Anniversary Collection Releases This November

Star Trek's 60th anniversary has been an incredible celebration of one of the most influential science fiction franchises of all time. From exciting new collectibles and original stories to the return of iconic characters from across six decades of Trek history, fans have been spoiled for choice throughout 2026.

Arguably one of the biggest highlights of the anniversary celebrations has been Star Trek's crossover with Magic: The Gathering, which brings together two massive fandoms and gives Trekkies an entirely new way to experience their favorite sci-fi universe. However, the celebrations are far from over, and Star Trek fans looking to expand their collections even further have another exciting release to look forward to before the end of November.

There are ten different designs available in the Mini Dice Cup collection:

The Mini Dice Cups are just one part of Sirius Dice's larger Star Trek collection, however. Enterprise and a Klingon Bird-of-Prey encased in transparent resin. Both designs retail for $54.99 apiece and could easily double as standalone display pieces.

#3321. Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

You’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most important tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

You can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

File size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

According to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

First, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

If you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

More importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

The DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

The Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

If you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for new hardware, this might be your best bet.

Xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

#3320. Frederick Wiseman’s Complete Filmography to Be Distributed by Janus Films

If you wanted to be a completionist for the movies of documentary legend Frederick Wiseman, or if you have a blind spot for Wiseman’s formalist portraits of American institutions dating back decades, today is your lucky day.

Janus Films has acquired the North American distribution rights to the complete collection of 45 feature films from Wiseman’s career dating back to his seminal “Titicut Follies” in 1967, and Janus plans to distribute all of them beginning January 1, 2027. Janus already has a library that includes the works of Agnès Varda, Ingmar Bergman, Akira Kurosawa, Chantal Akerman, and Edward Yang, so Wiseman finds himself in good company. Related Stories Movie Theaters in 2026: Filmmakers and Exhibitors on What’s Good, What’s Bad, and What’s Changing Mike Plante, Sundance Film Festival Shorts Programmer, Dies at 56

Specific distribution plans haven’t been announced yet, be it whether these films are going to be seen theatrically, via streaming, or on physical release. But Wiseman’s early films, everything from “Titicut Follies” in 1967 through “State Legislature” in 2007 have been restored in 4K by Wiseman’s Zipporah Films. “La Danse” (2009) through his final feature “Menus-Plaisirs – Les Troisgros” (2023) will be available in their original digital formats.

This is the first time any distributor other than Zipporah Films is licensing Wiseman’s work in North America, so the hope is that the late documentarian can now reach an even greater audience. It wasn’t until as recently as 2024, that Wiseman’s movies were even all available in digital formats.

“We couldn’t imagine a better home in North America for Frederick Wiseman’s films than with Janus Films,” said Karen Konicek of Zipporah Films. “It has been an honor to work alongside Fred for so many decades, producing and distributing his films. As Zipporah Films continues as the rights holder and distributor of the Wiseman Collection, we very much look forward to this new partnership with Janus Films and are excited to collaborate with them.”

“We are honored and thrilled to be the first distributor, in the US, outside of Zipporah Films, to be entrusted with licensing one of the greatest bodies of work in American cinema” said Peter Becker, President of Janus Films and Criterion. “We’re looking forward to presenting these monumental works, theatrically, to new audiences across the country.”

Wiseman passed away earlier this year in February 2026 at 96 years old. Not only was he one of the most influential documentarians in American cinema, he was one of the most prolific considering the 45 features he independently produced, directed, and edited over his 50-year career.

In 2016, Wiseman received an Honorary Oscar for lifetime achievement from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences Board of Governors for his “masterful and distinctive documentaries [that] examine the familiar and reveal the unexpected.”

IndieWire spoke with Wiseman in 2025 as Lincoln Center prepared a retrospective of all his early films as part of the 4K restoration effort. He spoke about the attention to detail in his editing and his examination of each institution and its layers, despite the enormous length of many of his films.

“The subjects I choose to make films about are complicated, and I think I have an obligation when I’ve been given permission to make a movie about a place to have the final film reflect the complexity of the institution and not just be some superficial, banal representation of the institution,” he said.

The full list of titles acquired by Janus for North American distribution is below:

“Titicut Follies” (1967), “High School” (1968,) “Law and Order” (1969), “Hospital” (1970), “Basic Training” (1971), “Essene” (1972), “Juvenile Court” (1973), “Primate” (1974), “Welfare” (1975), “Meat” (1976), “Canal Zone” (1977), “Sinai Field Mission” (1978), “Manoeuvre” (1979), “Model” (1980), “The Store” (1983), “Deaf” (1986), “Blind” (1986), “Racetrack” (1985), “Adjustment & Work” (1986), “Multi-handicapped” (1986), “Missile” (1987), “Near Death” (1989), “Central Park” (1990), “Aspen” (1991), “Zoo” (1993), “High School II” (1994), “Ballet” (1995), “La Comédie-Française ou L’amour joué” (1996), “Public Housing” (1997), “Belfast, Maine” (1999), “Domestic Violence” (2001), “Domestic Violence 2” (2002), “The Last Letter” (2002), “State Legislature” (2007), “La Danse: The Paris Opera Ballet” (2009), “Boxing Gym” (2010), “Crazy Horse” (2011), “At Berkeley” (2013), “National Gallery” (2014), “In Jackson Heights” (2015), “Ex Libris: The New York Public Library” (2017), “Monrovia, Indiana” (2018), “City Hall” (2020), “A Couple” (2022), and “Menus-Plaisirs, les Troisgros” (2023).

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. #3316. The Official Chronology and Reading Order of Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere

Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere is a multi-genre shared literary universe that has been going on since 2005. The premise is that thousands of years ago, in a far-away galaxy, a god known as Adonalsium shattered into 16 pieces called Shards. These Shards found their way to different planets in the galaxy, imbuing them with unique magic systems. Each stand-alone story or series is set on its own planet, with each world varying greatly in terms of culture, ecology, and geography. Yet, they do all connect in some way or another.

The Cosmere is planned to be a multi-decade event, and is not expected to conclude anytime soon. Currently, it consists of 33 entries, including short stories, novellas, novels, graphic novels, and even children's picture books. 33 stories to read is quite overwhelming at first glance, so if you've been looking for a place to start, look no further, because this is the definitive chronology and reading order of the Cosmere.

The great thing about the Cosmere is that it's engineered to feature multiple entry points — you can generally pick it up from any series or stand-alone story you want and still understand things. Sanderson's debut novel, and the first Cosmere novel to be released, was Elantris in 2005, which many fans use as an entry point to the universe. However, seasoned fans do not recommend going this route, as Sanderson's writing is less refined. Instead, many fans suggest picking up the first era of Mistborn as an entry point, as it is more accessible, enticing, easier to read, and generally more exciting.

However, another viable entry point is the White Sand graphic novel. Originally, White Sand was released as a trilogy, but the canon version is the omnibus version, which includes the original three plus an additional prologue sequence. While a lot of fans don't like White Sand as a story, it is a perfectly good graphic novel and highly important to the overall Cosmere. As it currently stands, White Sand is also the first story in the chronology, occurring before Elantris.

If you really wanted to, though, you could start with Warbreaker, The Stormlight Archive, or any other stand-alone novel, but beginning with White Sand, Elantris, or Mistborn definitely grants a more streamlined approach and makes it easier to hop from one story to the next without needing to jump back and forth through the chronology. On his official website, Sanderson actually recommends reading the books in release order if in doubt, which is a crystal-clear recommendation that doesn't convolute things more than necessary.

The "main" saga of the Cosmere begins with era one of Mistborn. This is followed by the stand-alone novel Warbreaker, which serves as a necessary prequel to The Stormlight Archive. Incidentally, this is what comes next, as the first arc of Stormlight occurs between the two eras of Mistborn. In fact, the final novel in Stormlight's first arc provides a smooth liaison to the second era of Mistborn.

Both of these series consist of multiple novels, as well as various short stories and novellas, which typically serve to fill the gaps between the main novels. Some recommend only reading the short stories or novels after you've finished the main novels in the series, but this isn't strictly necessary: they can be read in the order they chronologically occur, as well.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

"Hoid's Travails" is the informal name given to a trilogy of "Secret Projects" that Sanderson wrote while in quarantine. These three novels are Tress of the Emerald Sea, Yumi and the Nightmare Painter, and The Fires of December, which just came out for backers and is expected to arrive in bookstores soon. This series is more a loose collection of stand-alone novels, each taking place on a different, minor world, with Hoid narrating the story. Other secret projects include The Sunlit Man and Isles of the Emberdark, though these are distinct entities from Hoid's Travails.

The Sunlit Man absolutely has to be read after Stormlight, or readers will find themselves completely and utterly devoid of context. Also note that when it comes to Isles of the Emberdark, a revised version of the novella Sixth of the Dusk is fully integrated with the novel, so, assuming you read Isles of the Emberdark, Sixth of the Dusk can safely be skipped outright. There are also four picture books, dubbed "Hoid's Storybook Collection," that have just come out, best read alongside The Stormlight Archive because Hoid tells three of the stories to characters from that series, and the picture books are just illustrated versions of his fables. The fourth picture book, The ChasmFriends Get a Pet!, is non-canon and can safely be ignored, although it is a fun read.

Other than that, all that's left is the novellas The Emperor's Soul and Shadows for Silence: In the Forests of Hell. Truth be told, you can read these stand-alone tales pretty much whenever you want. They do have a place in the chronology, but you ultimately won't miss out on anything if you read them first or last. Note that most novellas and short stories can be found contained in a single volume, titled Arcanum Unbounded: The Cosmere Collection.

With the information available, it can be inferred that this is the chronological order of all Cosmere stories, including graphic novels, novels, novellas, picture books, and short stories:

This chronology is based on a combination of fan speculation and official word from Sanderson himself, though it is by no means the final timeline. As the Cosmere evolves, this timeline is subject to change. Buckle up, because it's been estimated that Sanderson is only about halfway done with the saga, if not a little bit less than that. It is known that a forthcoming series titled Dragonsteel is set to be the first chronological entry, even before White Sand, while the forthcoming final era of Mistborn is set to be the conclusion to the universe itself. These releases are pretty far away, however, so there's no need to worry about those just yet.

All of this can seem overwhelming, but if it's any reassurance, there really is no "right" way to read the books. Obviously, make sure you read each individual series in order, but other than that, you basically have free rein when it comes to entry and exit points.

If you're shopping for an iPad this holiday season, you might be a bit intimidated by Apple's price tags. The iPad mini starts at $599; the base iPad Air is $749; and the entry-level iPad Pro is a whopping $1,199. Most of Apple's iPad line certainly lives up to its expensive reputation.

That's where the iPad A16 comes in. This is Apple's least expensive tablet, with an MSRP of $449. But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

The iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

The iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Apple says this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee plans to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

As a huge fan of the design of the Air, and the functionality of the 18 Pro, Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone model could prove the perfect model for me. And for anyone else not opting for iPhone Duo 2.

#3310. 8 Saddest ‘Calvin and Hobbes’ Comic Strips of All Time, Ranked

Bill Watterson's Calvin and Hobbes is like few other comic strips. Sure, it's funny, with a decade's worth of moments following an unaging Calvin and his stuffed tiger Hobbes as they navigate their suburban life. Despite his young age, Calvin is smarter than other kids. He's a boy who lives in his imagination and loves to cause chaos.

His intelligence, however, has also led to many heartbreaking strips. Watterson, like Charles M. Schulz did with Peanuts, took his own grown-up anxieties and shared them through the confused eyes of an innocent child. Calvin is often happy and confident, so it's absolutely gut-wrenching to see him sad in these eight strips.

Calvin only has one friend in the world, and he isn't real. He could have an actual human friend, his next-door neighbor, Susie, but because she's a girl, Calvin rejects the idea nearly every time. To him, girls are gross and aren't allowed in the club he has with Hobbes. Deep down, he really does like her, though, as shown in how Hobbes is smitten with her, and he feels bad about how mean he is.

He won't tell her that. All Susie wants is a friend. She's just as lonely as Calvin is, and for her effort, she's constantly rejected and made fun of. In this strip, she lets her anger out. She can't believe how he treats her and tries to tell herself that she doesn't need him as a friend. Then comes the final panel of Susie playing by herself. It's not enough.

Calvin has a complicated relationship with his parents. He genuinely loves them, and there are some adorably sweet strips of them together as a loving family. With his wild imagination and non-stop energy, he also drives them nuts, especially his dad. Calvin's father is a man of rules. Most often, he wants to just be left alone, with all of his advice being about building character.

Usually, he takes it and doesn't react much when Calvin annoys him. In this strip, that's not the case. When Calvin breaks his binoculars, he goes off, screaming his lungs out in a rage. In a rare moment, Calvin's confidence breaks, and he cries, leaving his father shaken. He knows he has crossed a line and hurt his son.

Without ever explicitly saying it, Calvin and Hobbes portrays its lead as a lonely boy with no friends. He lives in his imagination, a place he can mold into anything he wants it to be. This strip shows that part of his loneliness comes from his home life. Mom and Dad aren't bad people by any means, but they're also so wrapped up in their own lives that they forget to pay attention to their son.

Here, in a stunningly drawn Sunday strip, Calvin tries to zap his dull parents into something more interesting by turning them into monsters. When they dismiss his antics, an upset Calvin goes upstairs and stares out his window. He turns his world into a far-off planet in his mind. Instead of making him feel better, the visuals only deepen his despair. Far off is exactly how he feels.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Calvin mocks so many things. Pretty much every human — and their confusing behavior — frustrates him. You'll never find him doing that with animals, though. We can see how much he loves all creatures, great and small, through his friendship with Hobbes. His stuffed tiger is his everything.

In this strip, it's only two simple panels that say it all by saying so little. Calvin is bewildered by how mean people are. It'll be okay, because Hobbes is here, and animals are a comfort. Calvin feels how many of us do. If we're having a bad day, all we have to do is hug our dog or cat, and we instantly feel better.

Calvin and Hobbes is not afraid to look at death, as these next few examples will show. Here, with the added panels of a Sunday entry, we get an extended conversation between two friends after they find a dead bird. Rather than being overly upset, Calvin is in awe of how beautiful and delicate life can be.

We're all going to die, and it could happen at any moment. Just as upsetting is knowing that the fear of death causes us to do all we can to avoid thinking about it. Calvin can't stop his thoughts. His only hope is that he'll figure it out when he becomes an adult. Bill Watterson knows he won't.

Calvin and Hobbes' most painful strips are a story told over several days when Calvin and Hobbes find a sick raccoon while out exploring. Desperate to save it, Calvin gets his parents to take it in. Surely the grownups can fix it and make everything okay.

They can't. Here, his dad must tell Calvin that the raccoon has passed away. Gone is the father who gets easily upset or completely ignores his son. He puts his arm around Calvin, being thoughtful with his words about how the raccoon didn't die alone. Calvin accepts this, but he can't let go. That vulnerable, innocent animal got into his very soul.

In the same raccoon storyline, Calvin is processing his grief about the dead raccoon. He's no longer crying his eyes out. Now he's working through the wise words his mother shared with him. Like his dad previously, she hasn't dismissed her son for caring. She also hasn't sugar-coated anything or acted like she has all the answers.

All living things are born and die. The only thing we can do is try our best despite knowing so very little about our own world. Nothing makes sense, and that makes sense to Calvin. Death is unavoidable. Still, Hobbes is not allowed to die. Calvin needs his imaginary friend, who will live on as long as his owner believes in him.

Another expanded Sunday comic takes us into Calvin's greatest fear: reality. He lives in his mind with Hobbes for a reason. Calvin doesn't understand his world or his place in it. It's much safer to pretend in a world he can control. At school, that becomes harder because it's the only place where he can't take Hobbes with him.

There, Calvin is on his own. No one is there to help him when math makes him feel dumb. No tiger is there to maul his bully to death. At home, the commitments don't end. Whether it's homework, dinner, a bath, or going to bed early, the boredom of everyday life doesn't stop. When his mother kisses him and talks about tomorrow being another big day, it brings no relief. Is this all there is? Without Hobbes by his side in this rare strip, he can't take it.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3305. If You Loved 'Phony,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us. When someone close to us suddenly, imperceptibly shifts, it can be unsettling, especially because you can’t be sure what’s changed or why. Those are the waters where Hulu’s Phony swims, delivering a perfectly pitched dramedy about a teenager (Sam Nivola) who emerges from a brief coma convinced that his mother (a pitch-perfect Connie Britton) has been replaced with a double. If you loved the series (and similar shows) and you’re looking for more intriguing stories about doubles and impostors close to home, you should definitely watch Goodnight Mommy.

Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).

A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before. The boys also find clues that bolster their fears, including a photograph showing their mother posing with a woman dressed identically to her.

The boys’ attempts to force her to confess rapidly descend into a kind of madness, ultimately leading them to tie her to the bed in an effort to force her to admit she’s not their real mother. It all leads to a reveal as affecting as Phony’s ultimate explanation (albeit a lot more grim and violent). The film goes way harder than the series, but if you were totally into the premise, this is the more horrifying version you’ll want to see. The original film is German; there was a 2022 remake starring Naomi Watts, and while it's pretty good, the original is the right choice. Stream Goodnight Mommy on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more impostor stories that dig into the psychological and emotional impact of suspecting someone has been replaced? Here are a few more movies that dig into the concept.

The Hole in the Ground offers an inversion: A mother who becomes convinced that her son has been replaced by an impostor. Firmly in the supernatural horror genre, the story still plays the same game with the viewer: Is Sarah (Seána Kerslake) crazy, or has her son, Chris (James Quinn Markey), been replaced by a creature living in the woods near their home? It’s got the same disturbing energy as Sarah struggles with how much her son’s changed behavior is her own psychological projection and how much is clear evidence that he’s no longer the same person—or, possibly, even the same species. Stream The Hole in the Ground on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Taking a slightly more literary approach (it’s based on a novella by Fyodor Dostoyevsky), The Double explores what happens if you find yourself replaced by a doppelgänger. Simon (Jesse Eisenberg) is a nonentity—ignored at work, lonely, and silently longing for the girl living across the street, Hannah (Mia Wasikowska). One day, a new employee named James appears at Simon’s job—and James looks exactly like Simon. But James is assertive, confident, and charming, sending Simon into a spiral. As the two versions slide into a battle for dominance, Simon finds himself turning to increasingly deranged moves to rid himself of the new and improved version of himself. If you loved the psychological implications that Phony explores, check out The Double. Stream The Double on Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

On one level, Denis Villeneuve’s 2013 film is about a college professor named Adam (Jake Gyllenhaal) who discovers an actor named Anthony who looks exactly like him (also played by Gyllenhaal). When he tracks his double down, their lives merge in messy ways, ending in tragedy and one of the most striking (and confusing) final shots in cinema history. On another level, Enemy is a deft trick, exploring someone’s subconscious using dream logic and misdirection. If the best part about Phony was the disorienting sense that a secret just under the surface will explain everything, Enemy is the perfect choice. Stream Enemy on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for a deeper, crazier, and more terrifying story about doubles, Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 film is a terrific choice. Inspired in part by his own feelings in the wake of a painful divorce, the story follows Mark (Sam Neil), a spy who returns to West Berlin at the height of the Cold War only to find out his wife, Anna (Isabelle Adjani), has been having an affair and wants a divorce. But Anna’s behavior becomes increasingly strange, and then Mark meets their son’s teacher, Helen, who looks just like Anna. And that’s before Anna kind of ... grows a replacement Mark from a tentacled creature kept in her bathroom (and that’s just the beginning of how weird this movie gets), resulting in two doubles. How much of the film is meant literally and how much simply represents the trauma of romantic betrayal and divorce is up to you, but Possession will definitely leave a mark. Stream Possession on Shudder, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Obsession looks at the Doppelgänger Effect from a different perspective. Cliff Robertson plays Michael Courtland, a wealthy businessman whose wife (Geneviève Bujold) and young daughter, Amy (Wanda Blackman), are kidnapped in 1959. When he follows police advice against delivering the ransom, both appear to be killed in an explosion. Courtland spends the next 16 years hating himself, until he encounters a young woman, Sandra (also Bujold), who looks almost exactly like his late wife. He works to make Sandra look as much like his wife as possible, and eventually proposes—but then Sandra is kidnapped in precisely the same way as his wife and daughter sixteen years before. This all leads to a head-spinning series of reveals and a twist that echoes the Hitchcock classic Vertigo. Rent Obsession on Prime Video.

#3304. Prime Video's 'The Mummy' Replacement 'Masters of the Universe' Is Officially a Streaming Hit

Jeffrey is a freelance features writer at Collider. He is an MPA-accredited entertainment journalist and a Tomatometer-approved critic based in the LA area. He graduated from the University of Texas at Austin with a Bachelor of Science in Radio, TV, & Film and a Bachelor of Arts in Theater.

Moviegoers eagerly awaiting the return of The Mummy franchise with next year's The Mummy: Book of the Dead can tide themselves over with another fun action-adventure with heart: the streaming smash hit Masters of the Universe. Based on the iconic 1980s Mattel toy line and Filmation animated series, Masters of the Universe wasn't a box office success, but it's finding a much bigger audience on streaming, topping the Nielsen streaming charts after its Prime Video debut. Fans who love high-octane action-adventure stories that are still full of humor, emotion, and genuine stakes, in the vein of The Mummy, will definitely want to check out Masters of the Universe.

What was interesting about The Mummy was how it veered away from the horror genre of its source material, the original 1932 movie. Instead, the 1999 reboot adopted more of an action-adventure, vintage serial movie style, evoking Steven Spielberg's Indiana Jones movies, with the addition of a slightly more modern vibe and voice within the period setting. That imbued The Mummy reboot with a unique and infectious effervescence that makes it so entertaining to watch.

Masters of the Universe follows a similar playbook: an action-adventure movie that takes itself fairly seriously, but still knows how to have fun and not become overly self-serious. That tone aligns perfectly with the source material, especially considering how silly and goofy the Filmation series could be. Thankfully, director Travis Knight updates the original cartoon's humor, aging it up, resulting in a movie that feels fresh and new, but still speaks to the child in you that loves He-Man and the Masters of the Universe.

Not to mention, Masters of the Universe features incredibly charming leads with Nicholas Galitzine as Adam/He-Man and Camila Mendes as Teela, who showcase wonderful chemistry. Their dynamic evokes the sparks that Brendan Fraser and Rachel Weisz created with their romance in The Mummy as Rick O'Connell and Evelyn Carnahan. The movie presents Adam as a comedically inept young man and HR worker who doesn't look or act like the traditional hero. However, Knight and screenwriter Chris Butler excellently craft Adam with depth as someone who yearns to return to his home planet and must become the legendary He-Man to defend it.

True, Masters of the Universe was born from a 1980s toy line, but therein lies the fun. The movie captures the childlike imagination and whimsy of dumping your action figures in a sandbox and letting your imagination unfold. Part of the joy of the vintage toys was rooted in how they were purposefully designed with their own lore, mythology, and history, providing kids with a jumping-off point to create their own stories within Eternia. Travis Knight, who has already proven he works well with similar material such as the Transformers spin-off Bumblebee, and other fantasy adventures such as Kubo and the Two Strings and Wildwood, truly brings the world of Eternia to life onscreen.

Knight imbues every frame with pure joy, awe, and wonderment, with a visual fidelity to the source material that most adaptations of existing IP and comic book superhero movies lack, right down to the colors of characters' costumes. For fans who grew up with Masters of the Universe, it was an absolute joy to see Eternia, Castle Grayskull, Snake Mountain, and many classic characters brought to vivid life onscreen and faithfully resemble their action figure and animated counterparts. When Adam finally held aloft his magic sword and said the words, "I have the power," becoming He-Man, it was a 10/10 moment with no notes. Plus, the movie is beautifully enhanced by wonderful music composed by Daniel Pemberton, with guitar renditions by rock legend Brian May.

Although Arnold Vosloo is great as Imhotep in The Mummy movies, sometimes the films focused more on cutting-edge visual effects and Imhotep as a CGI monster than creating a genuine threat and epic cinematic villain. But one area where Masters of the Universe outdoes The Mummy is its antagonist: Skeletor (Jared Leto). Make no mistake, Skeletor is the true star of Masters of the Universe, and the new movie excellently realizes the unparalleled overlord of evil with a mix of great practical costume work and digital effects. The CGI enhancement that realizes Skeletor’s bony visage is executed to perfection.

Leto's performance as Skeletor evokes the Filmation series' version, down to the way he constantly derides his minions. However, the new movie still treats Skeletor as a genuine threat despite his maniacal mirth; Leto brings both humorous charisma and genuine menace to Skeletor in a lethal combination. In recent times, it's rare for a major blockbuster to depict a fun villain who unapologetically embraces villainy. So it's great, for once, to have a villain who is evil simply because he enjoys it. Like he says in the movie, "I am the villain. And mmm, does it feel good!"

The Mummy: Book of the Dead will be out in theaters on October 15, 2027. In the meantime, you can check out Masters of the Universe, which is streaming now on Prime Video.

#3302. This Apple Watch Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

#3298. Why Black Friday and Cyber Monday Are Bad Days to Impulse Buy Electronics

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Some Cyber Monday deals are still live, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Follow our live blog to stay up-to-date on the best sales we find.

Browse our editors’ picks for a curated list of our favorite sales on laptops, fitness tech, appliances, and more.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a big "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be said for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before new models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The issue isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

The key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a new tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

To avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

If you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

A frantic search is underway for 6 people, including 2 young children, after a plane plunged into the waters off the coast of Mississippi ... just 2 days before Thanksgiving.

The U.S. Coast Guard says the single-engine Cessna was carrying 4 adults and 2 children when it went down Tuesday afternoon near Horn Island, according to CNN.

Crews have already made some alarming discoveries ... locating the plane's cabin, 3 life jackets and a life raft, according to CNN -- but there's still no sign of anyone who was on board.

WLOX reports the 2 children are boys between the ages of 8 and 10.

The plane had taken off from New Orleans and was headed to Fort Myers, Florida, when the FAA lost contact with the aircraft around 3:45 PM local time.

The Cessna was diving at 18,000 feet a minute in the final seconds before contact was lost, per CNN.

The Coast Guard has deployed boats and an aircraft to search for those missing. It's unclear what caused the plane to go down.

Horn Island made headlines earlier this year ... it's where the body of 18-year-old Nolan Wells was recovered in nearby waters following a Fourth of July outing with friends.

One of Amazon’s biggest sales of the year, Black Friday and Cyber Monday, is set to start Nov. 27, but many early deals are already rolling in. To take advantage of everything the sale has to offer, you’re going to need to be a Prime Member. If you sign up for an Amazon Prime account to take advantage of the sale but decide you don’t want to pay for an ongoing membership, you’ll need to cancel your subscription before the end of your free trial.

You can cancel your Prime subscription via web browser by first logging into your Amazon account. Amazon has a Cancel Your Prime Membership button on its support page to launch the process, or you can follow the steps detailed on Amazon's page:

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

As mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

Finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. And if you signed up for Prime through the Android mobile shopping app or the Prime Video Android app, you’ll have to go through Google Subscription to manage your membership.

#3291. Report: Apple job listings detail plans for autonomous AI agents

Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the company’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted new job listings that offer a closer look at its plans to develop autonomous AI agents:

In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the company could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how quickly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally launched its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

#3288. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3282. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.
