The best cheap cameras don't scrimp on quality

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Want to take great quality shots, but don't have the dollars to spare for an expensive camera? I've gathered together all my top picks for the best cheap cameras to help you out. I'm Pete, and I head up the photography testing team alongside Tom's Guide's reviews section.

The team and I have put our heads together to help you find the best cheap camera for you. Not sure what (or how) to choose? We can help there too, with loads of tips and tricks for finding a great camera.

There are plenty of options too, from mirrorless cameras to point-and-shoots — just think of your use case, and read our detailed breakdown of each model.

Pete is a Senior Editor at Tom’s Guide, overseeing the site's reviews team and all cameras coverage. He was previously an editor for Canon’s editorial site, and has been a photographer for a decade. Pete loves getting his hands on and rigorously testing the latest mirrorless cameras. He’s also the Tom’s Guide action cameras expert, putting each action cam thoroughly through its paces.

Nikita tests some of the best cameras at Tom's Guide, putting each camera through rigorous testing by pushing battery life to the limit, analyzing build quality and features to determine whether it's good value for money. She's also the in-house instant cameras expert as she has been using instant cameras since 2015, and drones expert as she’s a licensed drone pilot.

Ashley is a reviews writer here at Tom’s Guide and spends her time testing, well, everything! A lifelong photography enthusiast, she has a keen eye for detail. She's also Tom's Guide's resident ring lights expert — whether it’s golden hour selfies (she considers herself a professional selfie-taker!) or getting the best lighting for pictures of her dog, she is always putting lighting and camera gear through its paces.

Which type of camera do you need? That's important to figure out before you make a purchase. Here's a rundown of the ones that matter (we've included one of each in this guide).

One-line review: The Canon EOS R100 is the cheapest way to get a new mirrorless interchangeable lens camera (ILC), and its excellent image quality and solid AF make it perfect for budding photographers.

People who want to take photography seriously and have lots of creative control over their shots, whether they’re printing them or sharing them on Instagram. It’s ideal for anyone wanting an upgrade from their smartphone without breaking the bank.

The EOS R100 is about as affordable as mirrorless cameras get, yet still offers the essential perks of a “proper” interchangeable lens camera. It has a 24MP APS-C sensor which produces beautiful photos and 4K video. Combined with Canon’s excellent autofocus and the ability to swap lenses when creativity demands, the EOS R100 will give you everything you need to take Instagram-worthy photos.

✅ Beautiful photos: The EOS R100’s 24MP sensor produces beautiful photos with plenty of fine detail. In testing, we loved the natural colors this camera produces, rendering warm skin tones and vivid landscapes — this is Canon all over.

✅ 4K video: The EOS R100 isn’t a video camera, but will still shoot 4K at cinematic 24p, so if you want to dabble in a bit of video, you can!

✅ Great autofocus: Canon’s autofocus systems are legendary. And while the EOS R100 doesn’t have the brand’s very best AF with multiple detection modes (you’ll need the Canon EOS R50 for a taste of that), it still features human face and eye detection, making it great for portraiture and general use.

✅ Plenty of creative flexibility: This is one of the only cameras on the list that’ll let you change lenses (the other is the Pentax KF), which is a big deal. As you grow as a photographer, you can swap lenses to tailor the look and style of your photos.

✅ Solid build: Despite being lightweight and compact, this is a Canon camera, so you can rest assured that it’s built to a high standard and will give you many years of loyal service.

❌ Fixed LCD: The EOS R100 has a fixed LCD, which makes it harder to shoot at odd angles, as you can’t articulate the display to suit. It isn’t a touchscreen either, which means you can’t tap to set focus points.

❌ Limited detection modes: As mentioned above, the EOS R100 only features human AF detection modes, so if you’re after a camera for wildlife photography, we’d recommend something with a more expansive AF system, like the EOS R50.

The EOS R100 isn’t the most feature-packed camera, but packs in a huge amount of functionality and creative flexibility given its budget price tag. If you want a cheap camera to expand your creative horizons and improve your photography, this is the best one to buy.

"Simply put, I chose the EOS R100 as it's great at doing the basics and costs very little. What more do you need on a budget?"

One-line review: The Pentax KF is one of the only new DSLR cameras on the market and is great for budding photographers thanks to its weather sealing, IBIS and great real-world color replication.

This camera is perfect for beginners who want a DSLR to learn the basics on, but which will also grow with them — its IBIS and weather sealing will make it a good camera as you explore more genres and get more creative.

The Pentax KF is the best cheap DSLR because it’s essentially the only entry-level DSLR you can still buy new — making it the cheapest by default. It isn’t the most affordable camera on this list, but its U.S. price (under $600) is very attractive given the feature set. It features weather sealing for shooting in all conditions, IBIS for stabilized handheld shots, and face detection AF to nail portraits every time. It’s difficult to find an interchangeable lens camera with IBIS in this price range.

✅ Strong imaging: The camera has excellent color rendition, strong high ISO performance and did well in our challenging dynamic range testing, too.

✅ IBIS: In testing, we were able to shoot as low as 1/4sec without experiencing any visible shake thanks to the KF’s IBIS, which is rare to find at this price point.

✅ Weather sealing: The camera is weather-sealed, so you can take it out with you on adventures without worrying that it will be damaged if it starts to rain.

✅ Angled LCD screen: The vari-angle LCD screen can flip out and rotate 180º, and is ideal for getting shots at lower angles when using live view.

❌ Heavy: Since this is a DSLR, the camera is much heavier than a mirrorless camera. The KF gets onerous to carry after using it for longer stints.

❌ Autofocus can lag: Although the camera’s autofocus is generally effective, it may occasionally experience lag. This is annoying at times when you want immediate autofocus.

❌ Not one for video: The KF only shoots video at 1080p, so it’s not a great camera for vlogging or video, which is a shame given it has effective IBIS.

The Pentax KF is a great camera for budding photographers and provides great value for money. It takes great images and has an effective IBIS system, the vari-angle display is useful for shooting at different angles, and the weather-sealed body means it can go with you everywhere and not get damaged by the elements. It’s an ideal camera to both learn and grow with.

"It’s the only budget DSLR still being made, but it’s ideal for beginners learning the exposure triangle on a budget."

One line review: The Sony ZV-1F is packed with vlogging-specific features that make content creation easy, and it captures detailed 4K/30P video.

People who are stepping up from smartphone videography, hobbyists, and vloggers looking to take their video content to the next level. It’s ideal for anyone looking to replace their smartphone as their primary vlogging tool while being on a budget.

The Sony ZV-1F is packed with vlogging-specific features, like Product Showcase and Background Defocus, which are usually found on more expensive models. It’s perfect for on-the-fly content creation and to take traveling, thanks to its compact size. It also shoots lovely 4K/30P video, and its straightforward control scheme makes it extremely easy to use.

✅ Compact and portable: Measuring just 4.15 x 2.36 x 1.82 inches and weighing 0.5lbs, the ZV-1F is highly portable as it slips easily into most pockets, and it’s comfortable to hold with either one or both hands.

✅ Easy to use: With its straightforward control scheme and responsive LCD touchscreen, the ZV-1F is extremely easy to use, making the transition from smartphones to cameras seamless.

✅ Lovely video quality: The ZV-1F shoots 4K/30P video and 1080P footage at 5x slow motion by using 120fps. The results are sharp and detailed, and the camera’s autofocus system works well to keep subjects in focus.

✅ Product Showcase: Product Showcase works extremely well for product unboxing videos and reviews as the ZV-1F focuses on the subject closest to the lens while effectively blurring the background. For non-camera-savvy content creators, it makes it easy to create stylized footage.✅ Great built-in mic: The ZV-1F is fitted with a directional three-way capsule mic which captures crisp and clear audio, helping you create content on the fly even if you don’t have an external microphone.

❌ No IBIS: The ZV-1F doesn’t feature in-body image stabilization, which is fairly common in this price range. Instead, you’ll rely on Sony’s SteadyShot technology for capturing smooth and stable footage.

❌ Poor battery life: A single charge yields 360 shots when the monitor is always-on and 540 shots when Auto Monitor off is set to two seconds. This is much lower compared to the ZV-1F’s rivals.

The Sony ZV-1F is a fantastic camera for those stepping up from smartphone videography and looking to take their vlogging content to the next level — all while being on a budget. Its ease of use, compact body, great built-in mic and vlogging-specific features make it the best cheap vlogging camera.

"Easy: it's the cheapest way to get advanced vlogging features and make great-looking video content for social and YouTube."

One-line review: The DJI Osmo Action 4 is a feature-packed professional action camera that's cheaper than ever now that it has been succeeded by a newer model.

People who need a rugged video camera — that means content creators, YouTubers and vloggers, shooting video outdoors, especially if it’s high octane.

The DJI Osmo Action 4 shoots beautiful 4K at up to 120fps, and while YouTube (and most people's monitors) still max out at 4K, you really don’t need more. It’s waterproof down to 59 feet without a case (you’ll only get better than that with its bigger sibling, the DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro) and is built to withstand almost anything the elements can throw at it. It also has a front selfie display for vlogging, and a quick-release magnetic mount for securely attaching and switching between accessories, like selfie sticks.

✅ 4K/120p video: The OA4 shoots beautiful 4K/60p footage, for capturing fast-paced action. If you want slow motion video, it’ll also shoot at up to 120fps in full 4K. It also packs a range of professional features, such as Log recording.

✅ Wireless mic hook up: The OA4 can hook up wirelessly to DJI mics, such as the fantastic DJI Mic 2, giving you professional audio quality with no cables or adapters needed!

✅ An oldie but a goodie: The Osmo Action 4 has now been succeeded by the DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro, driving the OA4’s price down! You can pick it up for just over $200, which is about as cheap as professional-quality action cams come.

✅ So much ruggedness: The OA4 is waterproof to 59 feet, and is fully equipped to withstand the rigors of the environment.

✅ Front vlogging screen: Thanks to its front screen, the OA4 functions well as a vlogging and selfie camera.

❌ No higher than 4K: This camera tops out at 4K. That’ll be plenty enough for most people, but if you’re a pro shooter wanting to oversample 4K, you’ll be out of luck.

❌ Stabilization not the best: The OA4’s stabilization is decent, but not as good as the OA5 Pro or GoPro Hero12 Black. That said, it’s much better than other budget brand cameras at similar price points, like the Akaso Brave 8 Lite.

There's a reason the DJI Osmo Action 4 got the "Best Budget" award on our roundup of the best action cameras. Actually, there are a fair few reasons.

Despite being over a year old, it’s still an outstanding camera for the money, and will record professional-quality 4K video, with great internal audio, easy wireless mic hookup, useful vlogging features and all the ruggedness you could need.

Its stabilization isn’t the best, but it’s fine for most uses, and the lack of +4K recording likely won’t be a problem to anyone in the budget market.

"The DJI Osmo Action 4 is the cheapest way to get professional-looking, well-stabilized 4K/60fps action footage. There might be better action cams out there, but not for the money."

One-line review: Our favorite budget instant camera, the compact Fujifilm Instax mini 41 takes great photos, is incredibly easy to use, and it looks premium too.

Anyone who wants to print photos quickly and easily, without spending too much to begin with (obviously). If you want physical copies of your photos, it's for you. It’s perfect for documenting nights out with friends, weddings, and travels. It’s also quite the bargain given its features.

If you’re looking for lovely and detailed prints with accurate color reproduction, especially in bright conditions, the Instax mini 41 is your port of call. It’s easy to use, and it sports a sleek, premium design. Packing a long battery life as well as a selfie mirror and close-up mode, it’s the perfect cheap instant camera for most photographers.

✅ Easy to use: Sporting a straightforward control scheme that doesn’t feel cluttered, the Instax mini 41 is one of the easiest instant cameras to use. Every button is within easy reach, and each press gives good tactile feedback.

✅ Stunning image quality: Thanks to a maximum aperture of f/12.7 and a shutter speed of 1/2-1/250s, the Instax mini 41 takes lovely photos, especially in bright conditions. Printing and developing is quick at just under 90 seconds, and the photos look colorful and detailed.

✅ Long battery life: The Instax mini 41 utilizes two AA batteries, and the camera can last a total of 100 shots between charges. You can also use rechargeable batteries with it.

✅ Selfie mirror and close-up mode: For people who love taking selfies or like dabbling in macro photography, the Instax mini 41 features a built-in selfie mirror as well as a dedicated close-up mode, both of which work well.

❌ Flash always stays on: Unfortunately, you can’t turn off the Instax mini 41’s flash so it is always on regardless of where or what you’re shooting.

❌ Uses disposable batteries: Disposable batteries can be difficult to recycle so if you’re conscious about harming the planet, this might not be the camera for you.

Cheap and cheerful, the Fujifilm Instax mini 41 is packed full of features at a low price. It's compact and portable, and it looks sleek and premium. It takes fantastic photos in bright conditions, and it lasts very long between charges. Thanks to its ease of use and selfie mirror too, the Instax mini 41 is the best cheap instant camera for your money.

"The Instax mini 41's array of features will suit both casual and serious instant photographers. At this price, it's hard to find such a feature-packed instant camera."

One line review: The Kodak Charmera is a lovely little camera that’s extremely easy to use, and it clips on to your bag or keys, making it highly portable. If space is an issue, look no further.

Anyone who wants a cheap and extremely cheerful camera and isn’t fazed by the subpar image quality should get the Kodak Charmera. As it’s very easy to use thanks to a stripped-back control scheme, it’s perfect for even those who aren’t familiar with the semantics of photography. Oh, and it’s very cute and colorful, reminiscent of 90s tech!

The Kodak Charmera is the smallest camera we’ve tested, and it captures lo-fi images while featuring a straightforward control scheme and menu system. It can record 1080p video at 30fps too, making it a great travel or night-out companion.

✅ Extremely portable: The Kodak Charmera measures just 2.28 x 0.96 x 0.78 inches, and it weighs only 1.05oz, so it’s compact and lightweight. It features a keychain loop so you can hook it on to bags, keys and even jacket zips for easy portability.

✅ Array of filters: There are 11 filters and frames to play with and give your photos a unique look. The four frames feature film-like borders, vintage elements, and even a tiny computer screen.

✅ Lo-fi aesthetic: The photos captured by the Kodak Charmera have a lo-fi aesthetic with plenty of grain, which makes them look like they were taken on an old camera — something very popular on social media right now.

❌ Redundant viewfinder: The Kodak Charmera features a viewfinder but it’s too small and doesn’t display any useful information (unlike EVFs and OVFs on more advanced cameras). It’s less of a viewfinder and more of a hole in the camera.

❌ 1.6MP images only: With a small sensor and only 1.6MP at your disposal, the Kodak Charmera takes decent photos but they won’t win you any pro photography awards.

The Kodak Charmera is an excellent camera for people who want to capture images with a lo-fi aesthetic, and add filters and frames to them. Its ease of use, keychain design, and high portability make it the best cheap small camera.

“The Charmera is cute and lovable, and because it’s so small, there really is no better camera if you want to take one traveling or on a night out.”

One-line review: For the money, they don't come more hardy than the Kodak PIXPRO WPZ2, which impressed us with its competency, image quality and of course, its ruggedness.

The Kodak PIXPRO WPZ2 is perfect for adventurers and travel photographers who like to push their camera to the limit, but it’s also for those who don’t want to spend too much money on one. For $179, you get a rugged waterproof, dustproof and shockproof camera that produces good images and 1080P/30fps video, and it has decent battery life too.

The PIXPRO WPZ2 is waterproof up to 15m/49ft and it’s fully dust-sealed against fine and solid particles. It’s also shockproof and can take a beating, even if it’s dropped from 2m/6ft. This camera is, therefore, great for travel photography as it’s very portable. The PIXPRO WPZ2 is extremely easy to use too.

✅ Ruggedness: For just $179, the PIXPRO WPZ2 is waterproof, dustproof and shockproof, making it the ideal travel companion. It looks like an adventure camera too, with a ruggedly handsome design.

✅ Great photos: Although the camera is limited to taking just 16MP photos, the photos turn out detailed and have a vintage look to them. The camera also has a 4x zoom to aid in all shooting situations.

✅ Good battery life: The camera has a CIPA rating of 200 shots or 70 minutes of 1080P/30fps recording. For a camera of its (small) stature, this is respectable battery life.

✅ Compact & portable: The PIXPRO WPZ2 is also super compact, which combined with its ruggedness literally makes it a 'take anywhere' camera.

❌ Basic feature set: Similar to some other compact cameras, the PIXPRO WPZ2 has a very basic feature set which is limited to 16MP stills and 1080P video.

❌ Subpar low-light performance: The camera adjusts the shutter speed and aperture automatically and its low-light performance isn’t anything to write home about. The camera doesn’t show you how long or short the shutter speed is, which can lead to camera shake.

Overall, the PIXPRO WPZ2 is a fantastic outdoorsy camera that can be used underwater, on hikes in dusty conditions, and it can survive some falls too. Alongside this, the fact that it has good battery life and captures good stills make it the best cheap camera for outdoor adventurers.

"It's handsome and rugged, providing great protection against the elements, while offering the basic photo and video features you'll need at a low price."

One-line review: The Kodak Ultra F9 takes great photos and is incredibly affordable at under $50, making it the ideal starter film camera.

Fans of film photography or for those just getting started in it. Costing just $49, this reusable film camera produces lovely images in bright conditions, it’s extremely easy to use and is very compact and lightweight, making it great to capture holiday snaps on. The Ultra F9 35mm is fit for those looking to populate their social media feed with film photos.

Not only is the Kodak Ultra F9 35mm inexpensive, but so are film and processing costs. For $49, the Ultra F9 35mm is very easy to use as the camera adjusts shutter speed and exposure automatically, and photos turn out great with a retro touch and plenty of detail.

✅ Ease of use: The Ultra F9 35mm is an extremely easy camera to use thanks to the straightforward control scheme. It houses just two buttons so it can be used by anyone, and loading and unloading film is simple too.

✅ Great photos in bright conditions: The Ultra F9 35mm captures lovely images in bright conditions with a retro touch, and you don’t need to worry about adjusting exposure or shutter speed as this is done automatically.

✅ Low film costs: 35mm film is easy to procure and is inexpensive, as one roll (36 exposures) costs just $8 / £11. Processing costs are low as well, and it shouldn’t cost more than $20 / £17 on average.

✅ Lightweight and compact: This is a simple camera, which means it's lightweight, plus it's small enough to fit easily in a pocket.

❌ Can struggle in low light: The Ultra F9 35mm has a fixed f/9 aperture which is designed mainly for brighter conditions. However, it has a built-in flash for dimly lit environments and you can buy more sensitive film for low light.

❌ Tiny viewfinder: The Ultra F9 35mm has a very small viewfinder located right above the film door on the back. Those who wear glasses may struggle to look through it.

Overall, the Kodak Ultra F9 35mm is a fantastic choice for those starting out in film photography. It’s reusable so after the initial spend, you’ll just need to spend money on batteries and film — neither of which cost a lot. It’s easy to use, compact and portable, and it produces charming retro photos, all of which make it the best cheap camera for film lovers.

"This is my favorite cheap film camera because it takes great photos and can be used by practically anyone. It's the perfect way to dabble in film without spending much money."

One-line review: The Camp Snap CS-Pro is a pocket-friendly compact digital camera that we took quite literally everywhere in testing. It takes 16MP pictures that look pretty decent, but the big selling point for this is the lack of screen, keeping you firmly in the moment at all times.

The Camp Snap CS-Pro is the ideal for anyone who wants to capture their adventures. Because of the lack of an LCD screen to preview photos, you won’t be caught up in how your pictures look, and you can simply enjoy the moment. Any fans of the original Camp Snap Screen-Free Camera will love this model too, as the CS-Pro features quality upgrades (including double the sensor resolution) and four new color filter settings.

It can go anywhere with complete ease thanks to its compact size and light weight. Trust me, we tried. In testing, we took it to music concerts, on hiking trails, and out with friends. It held up in every situation and looked good while doing so. It may feel a little plasticky but this keeps the weight down. It takes great photos and demonstrated strong performance in a variety of lighting scenarios during testing, so wherever your travels take you, the camera will be ready.

✅ Color filters: The color filter dial on this camera offers four settings to add a little whimsy to the camera. This means you can even experiment a little with such a simple camera.

✅ Lightweight: At 5.12 ounces, this is one of the lightest digital cameras you can buy, making it ideal for throwing in your bag without being bulky.

✅ Easy to use: It’s a point-and-shoot camera, so there’s not much to it. But the lack of a screen means that you don’t even need to worry about how your shots look in the moment.

✅ Long battery life: It has a rated battery life of 500 shots, but we were able to get even better performance in testing.

❌ Shutter lag: This is vastly improved from the previous model, but there is still a shutter response delay when taking pictures in quick succession, which can prove annoying if you’re trying to get the perfect shot.

❌ Offset viewfinder: The viewfinder of the camera is set slightly to the left of the lens, so if you use this to frame your shots, you need to compensate a little, as your framing will be off.

The Camp Snap CS-Pro is the perfect travel addition for making memories without the distraction of a screen. Its small size and low weight make it a great option for anyone who doesn’t want a camera that takes up a lot of space. It holds up well in most lighting conditions and offers a reliable solution for fun photography with four color settings to choose from. It comes with me everywhere.

"The Camp Snap CS-Pro is the perfect choice for anyone who wants to make memories on a budget. The new model has even had a stylish looks upgrade, double the resolution, and new color filters that make photography so much fun!"

One-line review: A cheap and extremely cheerful point-and-shoot that feels like something from 30 years ago and takes lovely pictures.

Someone who wants to take snaps on holiday and doesn't mind if they can't see them until they plug their SD card into their laptop. This is about as "point and shoot" as it gets — if you want a screen to check things, you'll want something a bit different to this little retro hero.

The Camp Snap 2 is a super portable little camera, and it boils down the act of photography to its most basic parts. It's extremely easy to use — you pop your eye up to the viewfinder, point the camera at your subject, and press the shutter button. Its retro charm is hard to ignore, and the 500 snap battery life is good too. Oh, and it takes really nice images with a nostalgic twinge.

✅ Compact, lightweight design: Measuring only 1.3 x 2.5 x 4.5 inches, the Camp Snap 2 will fit into any pocket you like — and weighing only 3.8 ounces, you won't even know it's there.

✅ Super simple to use: Put your eye to the viewfinder and press the shutter button. This is about as easy to use as it gets.

✅ Good image quality: There's a wonderful retro charm to the images that the Camp Snap 2 takes — and they're bright and colorful to boot.

❌ Plasticky build: This is a cheap retro camera — don't expect sumptuous materials or premium build quality.

❌ Laggy shutter: Pressing the shutter button doesn't immediately activate the shutter. There's a slightly irritating delay.

This is a cheap, cheap camera that's packed full of fun features. The lack of a screen might seem like a problem, but it really reconnects you with the act of taking a photo — and the images themselves are great too. Why is it the best point-and-shoot camera? Because it does two things, and it does them both very well. It points, and it shoots.

"I love the Camp Snap 2 and its retro styling — the fun nostalgic filters are loads of fun too."

One-line review: Despite its tiny stature and budget price, the DJI Neo is absolutely stuffed to the brim with features and doesn't require FAA registration.

The DJI Neo is for drone novices or enthusiasts on a budget who are looking to enter the world of drone photography. For the features it offers, this drone is excellent value for money.

The Neo is great for those starting out in drone photography because everything is done automatically — from exposure to ISO. It’s extremely easy to fly either with your smartphone or the RC-N3 controller, and its small size makes it the perfect travel companion. The Neo is capable of shooting 4K video at 30fps and capturing 12MP stills. It has been succeeded by the DJI Neo 2, but that drone is quite a bit pricier, so we still favor the original Neo for this guide.

✅ Easy to fly: You can control the Neo either via the DJI Fly app on a smartphone or the RC-N3 controller, and both ways are straightforward. The RC-N3 comes with two detachable joysticks which are highly responsive and comfortable to use for long hours.

✅ User-friendly app: DJI's app is free to download and easy to use, while also providing lots of functionality and control.

✅ Compact and lightweight: The Neo weighs just 4.76 ounces which means you don’t need to obtain a license to fly it (but it’s still worth checking local laws before flying). This also means it’s very easy to travel with.

✅ Smooth 4K footage: The Neo shoots 4K video at 30fps or 1080P at 60fps, which is great for the price. Footage is smooth with plenty of detail, as is panning across a scene. Its f/2.8 aperture also delivers good results in moderately lit conditions.

✅ Very affordable: At under $200, this is one of the cheapest and best drones you can buy.

❌ Short flight time: On a single charge, the Neo has a flight time of just 18 minutes which is about half the time you get with DJI’s other drones. It’s worth investing in the Fly More combo which gives you two spare batteries to bump the total flying time up to 54 minutes.

❌ No obstacle avoidance: Unlike pricier DJI drones, the Neo doesn’t feature smart obstacle avoidance. This means that the drone can’t automatically dodge walls or trees, so you’ll have to be mindful of its position in the air at all times.

The Neo is a beginner-friendly drone that doesn’t cost a fortune, making it the ideal choice for aerial enthusiasts. The ability to capture gorgeous 4K footage and detailed stills, combined with its ease of use and lightweight body, makes the Neo the best cheap drone camera.

"The DJI Neo may not be the latest DJI beginner drone, but it still boasts fantastic specs and features for beginner pilots, all at a price that can't be beat."

Panasonic Lumix G97 ★★★★Considered for: Best cheap mirrorless cameraThe Lumix G97 is a great little camera, that produces solid images, offers decent handling and even boasts a form of IBIS (but only when paired with an OIS lens). Its AF is out of date for a modern camera, though, so we prefer the Canon EOS R100 for our best cheap mirrorless award.

Potensic Atom 2 ★★★★½Considered for: Best cheap droneThe Potensic Atom 2 is the closest competitor to the DJI Neo in the cheap, entry-level drones category. We loved its 4K video, 48MP stills, AI subject tracking and intuitive controller. At the end of the day though, the DJI Neo, which is also an epic drone, won for one simple reason: it's cheaper.

Pentax WG-1000 ★★★★Considered for: Best cheap rugged cameraWe liked the Pentax WG-1000 during testing. It shot decent stills and was indeed rugged. However, it's more expensive than the Kodak PIXPRO WPZ2 but doesn't offer much more.

Fujifilm Instax mini 12 ★★★★Considered for: Best cheap instant cameraAh, the legendary Instax mini 12. Make no mistake, we love this camera, and it holds the best for beginners award on our roundup of the best instant cameras. However, the Polaroid Go Gen 2 (holds the top spot on our instant cams roundup) offers a lot more for very little extra cash.

When buying a cheap camera, you’re naturally going to have to sacrifice a few things. The latest and greatest cameras simply don’t come cheap. Usually, you’ll either have to accept an older model, or sacrifice features.

However, you absolutely don’t have to sacrifice quality. You can pick up some great cameras for well under $100, and they aren’t just cheap crap. And that’s where we come in! This guide is designed to help you filter out the cameras that are cheap, yet still great quality and built to last.

The specific features you need to look for will depend on what you’re using the camera for. If you want to take really nice photos and grow as a photographer, then you’ll want a camera with a larger sensor, decent megapixel count and good autofocus — that means you’ll need to splash out on a DSLR or mirrorless camera.

Shooting video? You’ll want 4K footage, decent stabilization and the ability to connect external microphones. A vlogging camera is ideal, or an action camera if you’ll be shooting outdoors or in extreme environments. If you’re after sky-high footage, then you’ll want a drone (and yes, you can absolutely pick up great drones without breaking the bank).

Want to print your photos? You have a few options. The high-resolution sensors in mirrorless cameras will yield the best results when printing digital images. If you want the film look, you can go for an instant camera, which will be best for immediate printing and documenting social events, or a film camera, which will produce higher quality prints but requires film to be developed.

If you need a camera for travel, then it’s all about portability. You’ll want something that takes decent photos, but is small enough to fit in a pocket or backpack, and which won’t become a chore when worn around your neck.

Every single camera on this list has been through the Tom’s Guide reviews process, which means they’ve all been thoroughly tested by Tom’s Guide experts. The testing process naturally differs for the different categories of cameras — we test an action camera differently to how we test an instant camera, for example.

However, there are many things all cameras have in common. We always test how sharp the camera optics are, looking for optical distortions and image artefacts. We always evaluate how well images turn out, how detailed they are and the color accuracy of the camera. We take lots of test shots or videos with each camera, enabling us to test autofocus, exposure metering and all the extra features such as AF modes.

Naturally, we always evaluate the price of a product, test its build quality, and analyze both how easy the camera is to use and how sensibly it’s laid out. If there’s a smartphone app, we use it and evaluate how many extra features it adds, but also how user-friendly it is. We always evaluate the battery life of cameras, too.

We don’t just list the specs or features of these cameras either, and always analyze whether each of a camera’s features is good or bad, and why — that involves weighing it up against the product’s cost and competition. Throughout each review, we constantly compare each product to its rivals to help you make the most informed purchase. We’ve included links to the individual reviews for each camera within every entry, so you can get the full lowdown on each product if you want to know more.

Why spend money on even a cheap camera when you have your smartphone, right? Won't your phone take pictures just as well?

That depends on the phone and indeed the camera, but generally speaking a decent dedicated camera will be able to take better photos than your smartphone. Phones have small image sensors, as there isn't much space inside a phone case for a large sensor. The iPhone 16 uses a 1/1.29-inch sensor, which is a lot smaller than the APS-C sensor used in the Canon EOS R100. A larger sensor delivers cleaner images in low light. That said, many phones these days feature larger sensors than some cameras, especially compact cameras.

Another factor is optics. Smartphones have to use small lenses — again, as space is a major consideration. Smaller lenses just can't match the sharpness and quality of larger lenses on dedicated cameras, especially those on interchangeable lens cameras (like mirrorless or DSLR bodies).

And while some smartphones offer manual controls, often these aren't truly manual. You can adjust "aperture" on an iPhone, for instance, but the phone simply applies a software-generated blur to approximate the look of a shallow depth of field at wide apertures. While this looks OK at a glance, study the image closely and you'll see mistakes and things blurred that shouldn't be. This reliance on software is repeated in other areas by your smartphone camera, and generally results in poorer image quality.

And finally, there's use case. If you want to shoot film photos, or print your photos instantly, you can't do either with a smartphone alone. Using a dedicated camera is often more fun, too! There's something special about the experience of using a camera that smartphones can't quite replicate.

That really depends on the category of camera you need, and the definition of “cheap” changes based on said category. If you want the best image quality or a vlogging camera, you’ll need a mirrorless camera like the EOS R100, and cheap means around the $250-$400 mark. Action cameras, expect to spend around $175 - $200 for a cheap model.

Great instant cameras and compact cameras can easily be found for around the $100 mark, while affordable film cameras can be yours for very little more. If you want a cheap drone, you can expect to spend in the vicinity of $200.

No. Or at least, not until they're sure they want to get into photography. Cheap cameras are a great way to see if you like photography (or shooting video), and whether you really want to put in the time and dedication to learn and gain experience.

That's not to say you should buy the cheapest camera you can find, though, as there are many terrible cameras out there which are a total waste of money. You should buy a decent camera which will allow you to learn without breaking the bank. And that's where this guide comes in! It will help you choose a cheap camera that's also good quality.

#3182. ‘The Remarried Empress’ Star Shin Mina On Playing Royalty, Shooting In Europe & Why The Show Is Such A Huge Hit

EXCLUSIVE: Ahead of the finale of hit K-drama The Remarried Empress, Korean actress Shin Mina, who plays Empress Navier in the show, talked to Deadline about her experiences of playing the role and shared her thoughts on why the show is such a huge success.

She also shared some tips on what viewers could look out for in the final two episodes, which are dropping on Disney+ and Hulu later today (November 25).

Also starring Ju Jihoon, Lee Jongsuk and Lee Seyoung, The Remarried Empress has been a breakout hit in Korea and internationally, becoming the most viewed local original premiere of all time on Disney+ globally, just three days after its launch on November 3. Related Stories News Black Friday Streaming Deals Offered By Disney+, HBO Max, Paramount+, Peacock & More Casting Kelly Rowland Joins Hulu's 'Reasonable Doubt' For Season 5

Premiere views increased worldwide around 40% between its first and second weeks of streaming, with Latin America leading as the fastest-growing region, with views increasing by 43%, followed by APAC and EMEA at 39% and the U.S. at 37%. Watch on Deadline

Based on a Naver webtoon, the story revolves around Empress Navier and her dignified response when her husband, Emperor Sovieshu of the Eastern Kingdom, takes a slave girl as a concubine and suggests marrying her. While keeping her composure, Navier becomes closer to Crown Prince Heinrey, who can take the form of a magical bird. At the end of episode eight, we saw Navier inform her husband that would she accompany the Prince to the Western Kingdom to attend his coronation as king following his father’s death.

This was Shin’s first time playing an Empress in a romantasy epic, although she found some common ground with characters she’s played before: “I’ve appeared in a period drama before, Arang And The Magistrate, a fantasy-infused historical series, but I played a ghost in that one, so it was a very different experience from a traditional historical drama,” she tells Deadline.

“This time, even though the setting is an imaginary era, playing a character with a symbolic status in a world with social classes felt new to me. Above all, I loved that Navier’s dignity, strength, and wisdom are at the heart of the story. And I thought she was an incredibly proactive and appealing character, since in the end she chooses to remarry on her own terms.”

Shin admits she also got a kick out of wearing so many different styles of dresses. While Korean period dramas are usually filmed in traditional Hanbok, The Remarried Empress uses European-style costumes and sets and was filmed in castles and palaces in Germany and the Czech Republic.

“I wore so many dresses and tried so many different hairstyles. I kept thinking, ‘when will I ever get to film in dresses this gorgeous again?’ so I enjoyed every moment while acting. Of course, the costumes weren’t always comfortable,” Shin laughs.

But while she plays an Empress in a fantasy setting in the series, Shin says Navier is not so different to characters she’s played before: “There are seeds of love in Navier’s heart, too. As they slowly sprout, she realizes how she truly feels and chooses a new love. I think those emotional shifts, and the moments of facing love, connect with the characters in other romance projects I’ve played.”

On the huge success of the show, Shin says the popularity of the original webtoon meant that audiences around the world were looking forward to the adaptation, but that also put a lot of pressure on the cast and crew. “We knew many people were looking forward to the drama, but I’m sure some were also worried about a live-action adaptation,” Shin says. “So I was really curious how this new challenge would be received.

“When we started filming, I was worried about whether I could quickly immerse myself in this unfamiliar setting. But after shooting a few episodes, those concerns disappeared naturally. At some point, I was completely focused on the story unfolding within that world.

“Just as the cast did, viewers got immersed in this world and its characters faster than I expected, which was surprising and made me very grateful. I never imagined the drama would be loved this much.”

She says that, in particular, fans are cheering on the character of Empress Navier. “I think people relate to the situation Navier is in. She may look strong and cold on the outside, but she cares deeply for her people and shows warmth toward the imperial maids and Queen. I’m grateful that viewers understand and empathize not only with her human side, but also with the responsibility of living as the perfect empress and the pressure that comes with it.”

Shin adds that she enjoyed filming in Europe, and that shooting in real castles helped her get into character: “Being able to film in places steeped in another country’s culture and history felt very new to me. Wearing gorgeous dresses and filming in such exotic locations actually helped me become even more immersed in the world of the series.”

As for tonight’s finale, Shin doesn’t want to drop any spoilers, but has this to say: “I hope viewers will watch the finale wondering what the Eastern Empire will look like without Empress Navier. I also hope you’ll cheer on Navier’s future after making a new choice, the future of the Western Kingdom, and the future she will build together with Heinrey.

“Navier has always lived with genuine care for the Eastern Empire and its people. So I’d love for viewers to pay attention to what she feels as she leaves her homeland and chooses a new life, and to the emotions of someone standing at the start of a new beginning.”

In addition to Arang And The Magistrate, Shin’s previous credits also include My Girlfriend Is A Gumiho (2010), Oh My Venus (2015), Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha (2021), Our Blues (2022) and No Gain No Love (2024).

Produced by Studio N, The Remarried Empress is directed by Cho Suwon and adapted for screen by Yeoh Geena and Hyun Choongyeol. Ju Jihoon plays Emperor Sovieshu, with Lee Jongsuk playing Crown Prince Heinrey and Lee Seyoung as the slave girl Rashta.

We first got a glimpse of how big the show would become at this year’s Busan International Film Festival, which premiered the first three episodes to packed theaters. So far the producers are keeping mum on whether there will be a second season, but that looks like something the fans are hoping for.

The final two episodes are dropping today at 5:00pm KST, 4:00pm HKT, 8:00am GMT and midnight PST.

#3181. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

Silence the world around you with the best noise-canceling earbuds recommended by our audio experts

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

True silence when you're out and about is impossible — but you can get incredibly close with some of the best noise-canceling earbuds. Thanks to advances in active noise cancellation (ANC), they're great at keeping the noise of your commute at bay, and their in-ear design makes them super portable. But which should you buy?

At the moment, the best noise-canceling earbuds you can buy are the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. They've got the best ANC we've ever tested, and offer a comfortable fit so that you can wear them for long periods of time. There's little more we'd ask.

If they're over your budget or you need something you won't worry about losing as much, there's always the excellent CMF By Nothing Buds 2A. They don't cost anywhere near as much, but also offer great ANC and solid sound quality.

I maintain the site's buying guides for headphones, wireless earbuds, Bluetooth speakers, soundbars, and more. I have spent more than 20 years testing audio equipment for my own enjoyment, and was previously the Audio Editor here at Tom's Guide. There's nothing more I love than jamming out to my favorite tunes on audio equipment of different prices and sizes.

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 bring improvements to the formula across the board, in all but one key area. If you were to unbox your brand-new buds next to a pair of the old model, you'd be forgiven for wondering if you'd be shortchanged.

They look identical. All the way down to their eartip shape and silicone fitting wing, the QuietComfort Ultra Buds family is one that has a particular style that it has stuck with for a long time.

Pop them in your ears and you soon notice the difference. They've got even better ANC than the old model, with some of the most impressive noise canceling around. They block out everything — I took them on a long train journey, and found that all of the noise of my carriage was completely unnoticeable, even when not listening to music. It's like magic, as the orchestral sound swells and the noise disappears.

The transparency mode is very good as well, and it works well if you want to order your breakfast when you're going to work. The touch controls work well, and the charging case now contains a wireless charging coil so that you can more easily keep them fully charged.

Battery life is still not the best, though. Six hours with ANC on isn't quite up there, and four hours when you turn on 'immersive audio' is lackluster. It's not really worth turning the Immersive Audio setting on anyway.

It just thins out your music as it tries to distribute it around an artificially extended soundstage, and uses up an extra two hours of battery life. The soundstage is wide enough as it is, and the sound improved over the first model for some great audio as well.

They're still the best ANC buds you can get your hands on, and the Gen 2 just cemented their place in the annals of earbuds history. That ANC is just so good.

With the AirPods Pro 3, Apple was looking to unseat Bose's buds from the top of the list. Unfortunately for Apple, Bose released the refreshed Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 just before the latest AirPods hit shelves, but the AirPods Pro 3 are still a significant step up over their predecessors.

They've got sound to match the XM5, with a similarly natural sound profile and some extra juicy features that make them a whole lot more usable than the majority of the other options. They're a great jack of all trades and perfect for iPhone users.

The ANC is, Apple tells us, "2x as good as the AirPods Pro 2". In our testing, we've found that the ANC is, indeed, much better than the ANC of the previous models. It's better at blocking out sounds across the frequency spectrum, although it still focuses on the sounds you'll hear in your day-to-day life.

That means that bus journeys are more comfortable and office stays more tolerable. The transparency mode is natural-sounding as well and gives you more battery life.

There are some extra features on board the AirPods Pro 3. There's a heart rate monitor and Live Translation, although we found these to be novelty extras as opposed to 'reasons to buy.'

There are meaningful improvements in some other key areas, however. Fit is far better, and it seals very well in the ear to help the ANC. The battery life is excellent, with 2 hours more than the previous model, bringing them up to par with the Sony earbuds.

There are a couple of drawbacks. Android users won't like their less impressive features for their OS, but you were probably eyeing up the buds from Sony and Bose. There's still only one color option — white — and I've got AirPods that have died permanently gray after spending too much time in my black jeans pocket.

The AirPods Pro 3 are still an excellent pair of buds for iPhone users, however, and some of the best ANC buds around.

There are good budget buds, but there are very few as impressive as the CMF By Nothing Buds 2A. If you weren’t already aware, CMF is Nothing's most affordable product range, and the 2A sit at the bottom price rung of the brand's earbud lineup.

You might have thought that such a low price would mean low-quality ANC — but no, that’s far from the truth. The CMF Buds (sorry CMF, I’m not typing “by Nothing” every time) 2A are a budget revelation when it comes to keeping unwanted noise at bay.

We found that the sound of buses and other public transport was blocked very well by the buds, making sure that your commute is more comfortable. It’s adaptive as well, changing and shifting depending on the ambient noise levels.

Transparency mode was great when we wanted to order some lunch, with clear sound when we were chatting with the service staff. It’s not quite up there with the AirPods Pro 3 or the Sony WF-1000XM6, but then you could buy nearly ten pairs of these for the same price as either of those.

They’re comfortable too, with loads of fitting options in the box so that you can dial them in according to your specific fitting preferences. The battery life is solid with 35 hours on tap — that’s plenty to get you through a week's worth of work and commuting. Multi-point makes sure you can connect to different devices without the need to dip into the settings menu, and it works well.

They’re obviously not perfect — some compromises have been made to keep the price down. They feel a bit cheap, and there’s no auto-pause when you take them in and out of your ears. But again, when you consider the price, the few cons are very easy to forgive.

Sound is impressive, and there are loads of extra features in the Nothing X app like a customizable EQ. We love the CMF Buds 2A, and we think you will too once you’ve got the $30 wonders in your pocket — and you want to keep the noise of your busy 7:30 AM train at bay.

Sony has been trying to take the ANC fight to Bose since the latter released its finest, and sometimes Sony has come out on top. In this case, though, it’s the runner-up — but it's so close. There are still key reasons to pick up the WF-1000XM6 instead of the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2.

But about that ANC; it’s very good. We tested the buds in a range of different environments, from the office, a train, a busy city, and more. The noise cancellation kept out just about everything, and didn’t affect the sound of the music we were listening to.

It loses out to the QuietComfort in the smoothness of the delivery. That means that changes in environments are handled slightly more roughly than Boses pair, with a little noise leaking in before the algorithm takes notice. To be clear — it’s so close. If you don’t try both, you won’t notice. Side by side though, there is an edge to the Sony that’s not present in the Bose buds.

The sound, though, is better than Bose’s buds. There’s more delicacy up top, and they’re less low-end heavy. Sony’s tuning is more pleasing to our ears across a range of different genres, making them a better bet for the sound-quality-conscious. The AirPods Pro 3 sound even better, though.

They’re comfortable too, with a solid range of different tips for different ear shapes. The buds themselves a slightly strange shape, and the case is a dumb shape (it's covered with angles, so it’s less comfortable to fit in a pocket than the lovely smooth Bose and Apple options), but this is still a stylish and comfy pair of wireless earbuds.

Battery life is… fine. It’s unimproved from the previous model, the WF-1000XM5, with around 8 hours of use with ANC turned on. That’s more than the Bose buds and around the same as the AirPods Pro 3. Still, we’d like to see more battery life from flagship earbuds, considering how much you get with more budget buds.

So in the end, it all comes down to a couple of things. If you want the best noise canceling, buy the Bose earbuds. If you want something with great ANC that works with an iPhone, then get the AirPods Pro 3. If you want something that works well with everything, offers great ANC and excellent sound quality, then pick the Sony WF-1000XM6.

The Noble Fokus Amadeus bring a certain class to proceedings. They're covered in a very regal red colorway, and the buds themselves have a resin finish that makes them look almost like jewelry. And I love them.

They're super comfortable, especially if you use the flanged eartips. Those will also make your ANC better, and it was already really good. It blocked out the fan in my office, and makes bus journeys and train trips a whole lot more tolerable. It's not quite up there with the Bose ANC, but it does get close to the Sony XM series. That's impressive, especially given that Noble is a much smaller company.

The sound is the best bit, though. Slip them into your ears, and you're treated to the very best audio experience this side of $400. The highs are incredibly detailed, the mids are incredible, and the bass is impactful. They sound excellent — hence why they're on the list.

They lack some of the features of the competition, like the Spatial Audio of the AirPods and 360 reality audio you'll find on Sony buds, but they more than make up for it thanks to their incredible sound.

For audiophiles looking for their portable audio fix, the Noble Fokus Amadeus are the buds for you.

Fitness buds are a dime a dozen, with plenty of options available should you want to listen to music while you work out. The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the latest buds from Apple's subsidiary, and they also happen to be the best buds for fitness fanatics. They've got a useful fitting hook on each bud, and then heart rate monitors to make sure they stay in place.

The noise canceling, as you'd hope, is excellent. I found it perfect for most different settings, be that a quiet office or a bustling train. I'm not known for my exercise, however, so I spoke to someone who is — and what they thought of the noise canceling on board.

They took them for months of long running sessions and other fitness work, and found they blocked noise very well. Gyms silenced, annoying traffic brought to nothing. If you want to make sure your jogs, cycling, or even your swimming is distraction-free, then the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the buds for you.

I was also very impressed with the battery life of the buds. According to Beats, there are 10 hours of ANC on battery life out of the buds, and my testing proved that to be pretty much spot on. That extends to 45 hours when you put them back in the (very large) charging case, for some of the best battery life in the segment. It will depend on volume level and even genre, but expect good staying power.

Sound does trip up slightly. They've got plenty of detail and some fairly dynamic bass, but there's an unfortunate cut-off in the lower mids that takes some of the edge out of your music. For most people, it's not going to be a problem. But if you're picky about how your music sounds, you may be better off with a different pair of earbuds.

The heart rate monitor is useful if you want to track more of your fitness metrics, but we found that it wasn't the most accurate. Not a massive issue, but one worth noting.

In the end, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are a solid ANC option for everyone, but they're particularly good for those looking for a fitness companion.

Samsung’s buds have never topped best lists, but they’ve always had a space reserved. While they might not have the same “all things for all people” vibes as the Sony WF-1000XM6, the ultra-impressive noise canceling of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra, or the Apple user features of the AirPods line, there has been little better for users of Samsung’s phones than Samsung’s buds. They offer great performance at a slightly lower price and bring some exclusive features to the table, making them even better.

Noise-canceling-wise, you’re looking at performance that gets close to the AirPods and the Sony buds, just slotting in behind the QuietComfort Ultra. They do a great job of keeping noise at bay, as we discovered when we put them head-to-head with the Bose buds, and with music playing, you won’t find any horrible noises making their way through.

Transparency mode is similarly excellent, and doesn’t add the same robotic hue as cheaper buds. Perfect for when you need to speak to someone and don’t want to pop your earbuds out. In case you lose them. The algorithms that Samsung uses here are very good, and there are different levels you can access with the Samsung settings app and a separate Samsung earbuds application you can install.

Sound-wise, they’re very good as well, bringing plenty of bass and richness to the table. They’re a “big” sounding earbud, with plenty of depth. They’re similarly lovely in the mids department, making sure that music sounds great no matter the genre. Detail heads will miss out on some of the really high and clear stuff, but they’ll be better served by the buds from Sony. Either way, the sound is top-notch, even if it does focus on different parts of the frequency range.

Battery life is solid as a rock, although not quite as special as the likes of the Apple or Sony buds. Seven hours of staying power is plenty to get you through the work day, especially if you charge them in the case over your lunch break. The 30 hours of life in the case is actually better than the competition, which is always good, and makes sure they’re not going to need a wall outlet as often.

AI features are going to be useful for some and less so for others. Still, the likes of Interpreter and others are fun extras, even if you do have to have a Samsung device for them to work properly. If you’re looking for the perfect accompaniment to your S23 or newer, then the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are the way to go.

Wired earbuds are back, and there’s no bigger sign than Bose’s noise-canceling version of the format. It’s not the first time that Bose has made wired earbuds with ANC inside, but this version brings the latest algorithms to the table for excellent ANC performance paired with a reliable, tethered connection. They’re good to, although it seems that Bose is keeping some stuff back for either the more expensive wired option or to account for a lack of a dedicated power source for the mics and tech needed for ANC.

The ANC is good. Very good, in fact — we found that it blocked plenty of noise when walking down a street or working in a busy office. If you’ve not experienced the likes of the upper ANC echelons, these are going to be perfectly serviceable for everyday use. They’re just a little weaker than some of the other options on this list, with some higher sounds making their way through the barrier.

Transparency works well enough, making sure that you can hear what's going on the other side of the buds without all the extra noise around you. It does affect the sound of the buds slightly, however, so you’ll pay the price in sound quality when you’re ordering your McDonald's breakfast. The price you pay for a double sausage and egg McMuffin, one supposes.

The sound quality is a highlight of the Noise Canceling Wired Earbuds. The bass is less in your face than prior models, although it’s a lovely addition to the table. Similarly, high-range and lower-register mids sound great no matter the genre you’re listening to. It's a less in-your-face audio experience than previous Bose products, which is a nice change.

Then there’s the wire, which comes with both pros and cons. You don’t have to worry about battery life, for one. The power for the ANC is pulled straight from your phone or laptops battery, so your earbuds will only die when your listening device does. That’s good. You also get lossless audio thanks to the USB-C connection, and low-latency listening should you want to play games or watch movies and TV shows on the go without the sound getting behind what’s going on on-screen.

The bad thing? You’re tethered. Forget to unplug them or take them out when you stand up and you’ll send your phone flying across the floor or violently disconnect them from your laptop. You’ll need to get used to it, that’s for sure. But for under $100? It’s well worth the trade-off, if not only for effectively unlimited battery life.

We test a lot of noise-canceling earbuds, but not everything can make it into our buying guides. Whether that's down to better performance or stronger features from rival models in a particular category and price, some miss ranking in this list by the slightest of margins. With that in mind, these models are strong contenders and great alternative considerations.

Apple's new noise-canceling earbuds are here, and they land at a lower price than the previous model. We were impressed with the ANC this time around, although the battery life simply isn't good enough to kick it with the options above. Still, Apple users on a budget will find a lot to like here.

The ZE300 are Final’s lightest earbuds yet, and they’re perhaps some of the most comfortable buds out there right now. For less than $50, you’re getting excellent sound quality across many genres and highly effective ANC indoors, packaged into a pressure-relieving design with a comfortable fit.

A strong pair of cheap wireless noise-canceling earbuds, the EarFun Pro 3 deliver nearly 40 hours of listening (with their case), making them some of the longest-lasting among their peers like the Soundcore Liberty 4 NC. The ANC in the EarFun set is effective and the buds also support aptX Adaptive audio, and have a custom equalizer in its app. Our review also mentioned the good call quality and wireless charging.

Soundcore has finally joined the big leagues, although the Liberty 5 Pro Max aren't quite up there with the best yet. They sound good and offer some useful features, but we'd say you're still better off with the buds from Sony, Apple and Bose right now.

Read our full Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max review

We've judged the best noise-canceling earbuds on several factors: audio performance, battery life, Bluetooth range, call quality, comfort and fit, and the effectiveness of the noise cancellation. We also weigh special features, such as included apps, and how easy they are to use.

During the testing phase, our reviewers wear each pair of earbuds for 2 hours at a time throughout the course of a week, to test comfort over time.

ANC, meanwhile, is tested in both indoor and outdoor environments where ambient sounds are produced at high levels. This includes airplanes, city parks, convenience shops, offices, and public transportation. ANC earbuds programmed with transparency modes are also tested thoroughly to determine how well the listener can hear their surroundings.

For sound quality, we listen to many different sample tracks and span as many music genres as possible, including hip-hop, rock, jazz, classical and R&B, while evaluating volume, clarity, and fullness. Find out what we listen for during our testing process and how to get the best headphone sound for you.

And now that more streaming music services are offering high-resolution audio, be sure to read our audio codec FAQ for all you need to know.

Finally, we’ll rate noise-canceling earbuds on our five-point system, with 1 being the worst and 5 the best. If a pair is particularly excellent, with a robust range of qualities, we may award it an Editor's Choice badge.

The first item to check off the list when shopping for the best noise-canceling earbuds is their active noise cancellation performance, which shouldn’t be confused with passive noise cancellation. What are the differences?

1. Active vs. passive noise cancellation: ANC uses advanced circuitry and microphones to pick up noise signals and create inverse waves that cancel out these sonic disruptions, whereas PNC physically isolates high-pitched sounds through the headphone design and materials. Most headphones advertised with noise cancellation are categorized under ANC.

2. Battery life: Noise-canceling earbuds have a reputation for sucking up lots of power, so you’ll want a pair that holds a charge long enough to get you through a long business flight or weekly commutes. Noise-canceling wireless earbuds are usually rated for 4.5 to 8 hours, but with included charging cases the total possible playback time might be much more competitive.

Think about how long and how often you’d want to wear your earbuds for on lengthy trips. A longer “per charge” battery life is better, but if you only want some entertainment on short commutes then it not quite so important, as you’ll probably be storing the buds in their case more regularly.

3. Sound quality: ANC technology can compress sound and reduce dynamics, which may affect audio performance when turned on. In some cases, you’ll notice a background hiss when listening to music. However, the best noise-canceling earbuds limit these disruptions to deliver full, crisp sound.

4. Design: The look, build and feel of a pair of in-ear 'buds is massively important when selecting the best noise-canceling earbuds, so consider how they look and feel and whether the style is right for you. In our best noise-canceling headphones round up we mention that over-ear headphones tend to give the best noise cancellation, but some of the more recent wireless in-ear models are proving to be just as effective.

5. Pricing considerations: Obviously, price is a big consideration when looking for the best noise-canceling earbuds. Although there are always exceptions, big-name brands will typically command a bit extra, but generally speaking, the less you spend on a pair of headphones the greater the chance that sound and features will be compromised. Going for a budget option isn't always the best choice, as any money you save on your purchase won't do you much good if you're constantly needing to recharge your audio gear, or the sound quality is poor.

ANC explained: Active noise cancellation (ANC) models employ built-in mics to pick up ambient sounds around the wearer. An identical but inverted audio signal of the noise is played back to the listener through the headphones.

Listeners aren't aware of this happening of course, as the inverted (or out of phase) signal effectively 'cancels out' the noise of the surroundings for the headphone wearer. The process removes the external sounds, which results in a significant reduction in the level of background noise at the very least.

Given that it uses both more computational power and a bunch of microphones in order to work, ANC has an effect on your battery life. This often chops a couple of hours off, so they won't last quite as long. If you want to keep the battery going for longer then you'll want to keep the noise canceling turned off.

In most cases, noise-canceling earbuds are very effective at reducing ambient sounds. There are limits, though, and some designs are less effective at silencing certain types of sounds than others.

The process is fast but it can’t physically occur in real time, so active noise cancellation (ANC) works best with consistent low-frequency sounds as opposed to higher-pitched, inconsistent sounds like human speech.

Vehicle engines and droning air conditioners are easy to cancel out, but the shorter wavelength of high-frequency sounds, like a sudden blast from a car horn, makes it tougher for the ANC’s anti-noise waves to perfectly mask these bursts.

Even so, all sounds will be at least a little quieter when you’re wearing noise-canceling headphones, and many sounds can be completely silenced even on low-cost pairs or earbuds.

#3176. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety. Headquartered in Tokyo, Japan, the company provides automotive and robotics organizations with software and services to identify cyber risks early, assess their potential safety impact, and protect systems in operation, helping maintain safe, reliable behavior across real-world deployments.
